prog-dai-053.question: What percentage of biventricular pacing is targeted in a CRT patient?
options: More than 80%
More than 90%
More than 95%
More than 98%
commentaires: Incorrect: 80% leaves one beat in five unresynchronised, with a markedly smaller benefit.
Incorrect: 90% seems high but is still associated with a poorer outcome.
Incorrect: even 95% falls short of the target associated with the greatest survival benefit.
Correct: the greatest mortality reduction is achieved above 98% (Hayes et al.).
prog-dai-053.explication: CRT is effective only if biventricular pacing is almost continuous. The analysis by Hayes et al. (more than 36,000 remotely monitored patients) showed that the greatest reduction in mortality was achieved with more than 98% biventricular pacing. Even a rate of 90 to 95%, which seems high, is associated with a poorer outcome. Any lower percentage should prompt a search for a cause: AF, PVCs, an excessively long AV delay, loss of LV capture.
prog-dai-053.aRetenir: CRT target: more than 98% biventricular pacing.

prog-dai-054.question: Which causes may explain a fall in the percentage of biventricular pacing in a CRT patient?
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid AV conduction
Frequent PVCs
Programmed AV delay longer than the intrinsic PR interval
Programmed AV delay much shorter than the intrinsic PR interval
Atrial pacing at 60 bpm
commentaires: Correct: rapid AF conducts spontaneously to the ventricles and bypasses pacing.
Correct: these are unresynchronised beats, which can also place the next P wave within the PVARP.
Correct: the native QRS occurs before pacing, which is inhibited.
Incorrect: a short AV delay, on the contrary, promotes biventricular capture.
Incorrect: atrial pacing does not prevent synchronised ventricular pacing afterwards.
prog-dai-054.explication: Biventricular pacing is lost as soon as intrinsic conduction "wins" over pacing. Rapid AF conducts spontaneously to the ventricles. Frequent PVCs are unresynchronised beats and can also place the next P wave within the PVARP. An AV delay longer than the intrinsic PR interval allows the native QRS to occur before pacing; a short AV delay, on the contrary, promotes biventricular capture. Another classic cause is a sinus rate above the maximum tracking rate, leading to Wenckebach-type behaviour and then 2:1 block with intrinsic conduction. Atrial pacing at 60 bpm, by contrast, does not prevent synchronised ventricular pacing afterwards.
prog-dai-054.aRetenir: Fall in % BiV pacing: think of AF, PVCs, an excessively long AV delay and an excessively fast sinus rate.

prog-dai-055.question: A CRT patient is in permanent AF with only 85% biventricular pacing despite optimised rate-control therapy. What do the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend?
options: Stop CRT, which has become useless in permanent AF
Programme a longer AV delay to promote capture
Consider atrioventricular junction ablation
Switch to AAI mode to preserve native conduction
commentaires: Incorrect: CRT remains beneficial in AF if biventricular pacing is near-complete.
Incorrect: the AV delay is meaningless in AF, with no organised atrial activity to track.
Correct: the 2021 ESC guidelines (IIa) propose AV junction ablation to achieve biventricular pacing close to 100%.
Incorrect: AAI mode is impossible in AF.
prog-dai-055.explication: In AF, intrinsic AV conduction competes with biventricular pacing. When rate-control therapy is insufficient, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering AV junction ablation (class IIa) to ensure complete biventricular pacing. The AV delay is meaningless in AF, as there is no organised atrial activity to track. AAI mode is impossible in AF. Beware also of fusion or pseudo-fusion beats, which artificially inflate the pacing counter.
prog-dai-055.aRetenir: CRT + AF with incomplete BiV pacing: consider AV junction ablation.

prog-dai-056.question: A young CRT patient loses biventricular pacing on exertion: the trends show a sinus rate of 135 bpm with a programmed maximum tracking rate of 120 bpm. What is the most logical measure?
options: Raise the maximum tracking rate, together with a beta-blocker
Lower the maximum tracking rate to 100 bpm for safety
Extend the AV delay to allow intrinsic conduction through
Programme VVI mode to override the sinus rate
commentaires: Correct: raise the maximum tracking rate (checking that the total atrial refractory period allows it) and optimise the beta-blocker.
Incorrect: lowering this rate would worsen the loss of pacing on exertion.
Incorrect: extending the AV delay would promote unresynchronised intrinsic conduction.
Incorrect: VVI mode would abolish AV synchrony.
prog-dai-056.explication: When the sinus rate exceeds the maximum tracking rate, the device can no longer track every P wave: Wenckebach-type behaviour, then 2:1 block. In a patient with preserved AV conduction, the intrinsic (unresynchronised) QRS takes over, precisely on exertion. The maximum tracking rate is therefore raised, making sure that the total atrial refractory period allows it, and the beta-blocker is optimised. Lowering this rate would make the situation worse. Extending the AV delay would promote intrinsic conduction, and VVI mode would abolish AV synchrony.
prog-dai-056.aRetenir: CRT: maximum tracking rate high enough to cover the exercise sinus rate.

prog-dai-057.question: On the 12-lead ECG of a CRT patient, which appearance should raise suspicion of loss of LV capture with RV-only pacing?
options: Paced QRS with dominant R in V1 and Q wave in lead I
Narrow QRS with no visible spike, identical to the intrinsic QRS
Paced QRS with QS or rS in V1 and broad R in lead I
Retrograde P wave after each paced QRS
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the usual appearance of effective biventricular pacing (LV contribution).
Incorrect: a narrow QRS with no spike reflects intrinsic conduction, not RV-only pacing.
Correct: RV-only pacing activates from right to left, with a left-sided delay pattern: QS in V1, R in lead I.
Incorrect: a retrograde P wave gives no information about LV capture.
prog-dai-057.explication: With RV-only pacing (from the apex or septum), activation proceeds from right to left, giving an LBBB-like pattern with a QS complex in V1 and a positive R wave in lead I. With effective biventricular pacing, the LV contribution usually produces an R wave in V1 and a Q wave (or a negative pattern) in lead I. These criteria are not absolute (lead positions, scars), hence the value of comparison with the reference ECG recorded after implantation. Loss of LV capture is confirmed with the programmer by an LV threshold test.
prog-dai-057.aRetenir: RV-only pacing in CRT: QS in V1, R in lead I; always compare with the reference ECG.

prog-dai-058.question: In a CRT "non-responder" at 6 months, what is the first step?
options: Explant the LV lead and revert to simple RV pacing
Check % BiV pacing, LV capture, arrhythmias and medical therapy
Upgrade straight away to CRT-D to improve response
Programme the maximum AV delay to respect native conduction
commentaires: Incorrect: CRT is not abandoned before looking for correctable causes of non-response.
Correct: correctable causes are sought first, before any echocardiographic optimisation of delays.
Incorrect: the defibrillator does not treat non-response to resynchronisation.
Incorrect: a long AV delay promotes intrinsic conduction and loss of biventricular pacing.
prog-dai-058.explication: About one third of patients do not respond to CRT. Before concluding that it has failed, correctable causes are sought: incomplete biventricular pacing (AF, PVCs, inappropriate AV delay), loss of LV capture or phrenic nerve stimulation that led to the output being reduced, an unfavourable LV lead position (apical or anterior), insufficient medical therapy or volume overload. Multidisciplinary care improves these outcomes. Echocardiographic optimisation of AV/VV delays comes later, on a case-by-case basis. Upgrading to CRT-D does not treat non-response.
prog-dai-058.aRetenir: CRT non-responder: first check % BiV pacing, LV capture, arrhythmias and medical therapy, then the delays.

prog-dai-059.question: True or false: routine echocardiographic optimisation of AV and VV delays is recommended in all patients after CRT implantation.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: randomised trials have not shown any benefit from routine echocardiographic optimisation.
Correct: programming is empirical, and guided optimisation is reserved for non-responders.
prog-dai-059.explication: False: randomised trials have not shown any benefit from routine echocardiographic optimisation of AV/VV delays compared with empirical programming. In practice, an AV delay short enough to ensure biventricular capture without truncating atrial filling is programmed, and guided optimisation (echocardiography, ECG, automatic algorithms) is reserved for non-responders. The pitfall is to invest considerable resources for an unproven benefit, instead of first checking the pacing percentage and LV capture.
prog-dai-059.aRetenir: AV/VV optimisation: not routine, reserved for non-responders.

prog-dai-060.question: A patient with an LVEF of 35% and high-grade AV block requires ventricular pacing. What do the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend?
options: CRT rather than RV pacing, regardless of NYHA class
Dual-chamber pacemaker with conventional apical RV pacing
Single-chamber VVI pacemaker programmed at 40 bpm
No pacemaker as long as the patient remains asymptomatic
commentaires: Correct: LVEF < 40% and a need for ventricular pacing = CRT rather than RV pacing (class I in 2021, IIa in the 2026 ESC HF guidelines), even in AF.
Incorrect: in a patient with LVEF < 40%, frequent RV pacing worsens LV dysfunction.
Incorrect: VVI at 40 bpm is inappropriate for high-grade AV block and does not correct dyssynchrony.
Incorrect: high-grade AV block is an indication for pacing, even in a patient with few symptoms.
prog-dai-060.explication: In a patient with reduced LVEF who needs ventricular pacing for high-grade AV block, the 2021 ESC guidelines (cardiac pacing and CRT) recommend CRT rather than RV pacing (class I, level A, for LVEF < 40%), including in AF and regardless of NYHA class. Isolated RV pacing, even with a dual-chamber device, creates LBBB-type dyssynchrony that worsens LV dysfunction, especially if it is near-continuous. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines keep the same message, regardless of NYHA class and QRS width, but as class IIa (level B1), and for all HFrEF, now defined as LVEF < 50%. VVI at 40 bpm or no pacing would be inappropriate for high-grade AV block, even with few symptoms. Conduction system pacing is an evolving alternative; the 2026 ESC HF guidelines make no recommendation on it in the absence of a randomised trial with clinical endpoints.
prog-dai-060.aRetenir: Reduced LVEF + high-grade AV block = CRT rather than RV pacing (ESC 2021: class I; ESC 2026 HF: class IIa).

prog-dai-061.question: True or false: in a patient with a conventional pacemaker and a high burden of RV pacing who develops symptomatic heart failure with LVEF ≤ 35% despite optimal therapy, an upgrade to CRT should be considered.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: upgrade to CRT should be considered (class IIa) in RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.
Incorrect: the 2021 ESC guidelines do recommend considering upgrade (IIa), confirmed by the 2026 ESC HF guidelines, weighing up the procedural risk.
prog-dai-061.explication: True: the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering upgrade to CRT (class IIa) in this setting of RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines confirm class IIa (level B1) in patients with LVEF ≤ 35% and a significant proportion of RV pacing whose HF worsens despite optimal therapy. They are based on BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade, the first randomised trial on this subject: with ≥ 20% RV pacing and a paced QRS ≥ 150 ms, upgrade to CRT-D reduced the primary composite endpoint of death, HF hospitalisation and absence of reverse remodelling (HR 0.27). The 2026 ESC guidelines also recommend checking the proportion of RV pacing in any device recipient with new-onset or worsening HFrEF (class IIa). Upgrade (or conduction system pacing) restores more physiological ventricular activation. The procedural risk, which is higher than at de novo implantation, must be weighed up.
prog-dai-061.aRetenir: RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy with LVEF ≤ 35%: CRT upgrade (IIa, BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade); always check the % RV pacing.

prog-dai-062.question: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, how should one choose between CRT-P and CRT-D in a patient with an indication for CRT?
options: CRT-D routinely in all patients eligible for resynchronisation
CRT-D reserved for non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy
CRT-P routinely over the age of 75, whatever the context
CRT-D if there is an ICD indication; otherwise, shared decision
commentaires: Incorrect: in the absence of an ICD indication, the choice is individualised (class IIa).
Incorrect: the opposite is true; the benefit of the defibrillator tends to be smaller in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy (DANISH).
Incorrect: no strict age cut-off is set; age is only one element of the decision.
Correct: CRT-D is recommended (class I) if there is an ICD indication; otherwise, the decision is made case by case.
prog-dai-062.explication: If the patient has an ICD indication (secondary prevention, ischaemic heart disease with LVEF ≤ 35%), a CRT-D is recommended (class I). Otherwise, the choice is made on a case-by-case basis (class IIa): age, comorbidities, aetiology (smaller benefit of the defibrillator in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, especially in older patients, as suggested by DANISH), fibrosis on MRI and patient preference. CRT-P is simpler, less costly and carries no risk of inappropriate shocks. No strict age cut-off is set.
prog-dai-062.aRetenir: CRT-D if there is an ICD indication; otherwise, an individualised, shared decision.

prog-dai-063.question: Which trial showed, in NYHA III–IV patients, a reduction in all-cause mortality with CRT-D compared with medical therapy, whereas the mortality reduction with CRT-P did not reach statistical significance?
options: CARE-HF
COMPANION
EchoCRT
MADIT-CRT
commentaires: Incorrect: CARE-HF showed that CRT-P alone reduces mortality; it had no CRT-D arm.
Correct: significant mortality reduction with CRT-D, borderline significance with CRT-P.
Incorrect: EchoCRT involved patients with a narrow QRS and was stopped for futility.
Incorrect: MADIT-CRT involved mildly symptomatic patients (NYHA I–II), CRT-D versus ICD alone.
prog-dai-063.explication: COMPANION compared medical therapy, CRT-P and CRT-D in NYHA III–IV patients with QRS ≥ 120 ms. Both forms of CRT reduced the endpoint of death or hospitalisation. For all-cause mortality, the reduction was significant with CRT-D and of borderline significance with CRT-P. CARE-HF, published later, demonstrated that CRT-P alone reduces mortality. MADIT-CRT involved mildly symptomatic patients (NYHA I–II), and EchoCRT patients with a narrow QRS.
prog-dai-063.aRetenir: COMPANION: CRT-D reduces mortality; CARE-HF: so does CRT-P.

prog-dai-064.question: Which patients were enrolled in MADIT-CRT, and which subgroup benefited most?
options: NYHA III–IV, LVEF ≤ 35%, QRS ≥ 120 ms; benefit mainly with RBBB
NYHA I–II, LVEF ≤ 30%, QRS ≥ 130 ms; benefit mainly with LBBB
NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 40%, QRS ≥ 150 ms; benefit mainly in AF
NYHA I–II, LVEF ≤ 35%, QRS < 130 ms; benefit in women
commentaires: Incorrect: MADIT-CRT specifically enrolled mildly symptomatic patients, and the benefit concerned LBBB.
Correct: mildly symptomatic patients, CRT-D versus ICD alone, with the benefit concentrated in LBBB.
Incorrect: LVEF ≤ 30%, not 40%, and patients in permanent AF were not the target of the trial.
Incorrect: MADIT-CRT enrolled only patients with QRS ≥ 130 ms; a narrow QRS does not warrant CRT.
prog-dai-064.explication: MADIT-CRT compared CRT-D with ICD alone in mildly symptomatic patients (ischaemic NYHA I or NYHA II), with LVEF ≤ 30% and QRS ≥ 130 ms. CRT-D reduced heart failure events by about one third, and this benefit was concentrated in patients with LBBB. This trial extended CRT to mildly symptomatic patients. It reinforced the idea that LBBB morphology is the best predictor of response.
prog-dai-064.aRetenir: MADIT-CRT: CRT is beneficial from NYHA I–II, especially with LBBB.

prog-dai-065.question: Which ECG criteria are classically sought to confirm left bundle branch capture during left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP)?
options: LBBB pattern in V1, long LV activation time in V6
Paced QRS > 200 ms, with a left-sided delay pattern
qR in V1, short and stable LV activation time in V6
No visible spike and a QRS identical to the intrinsic one
commentaires: Incorrect: this pattern reflects deep septal pacing without left bundle branch capture.
Incorrect: such a broad QRS suggests slow myocardial pacing, far from conduction system capture.
Correct: right-sided delay in V1 (qR, rSR') and a short stimulus to R-wave peak time in V6 that remains constant as output is varied.
Incorrect: a QRS identical to the intrinsic one with no spike reflects absence of pacing.
prog-dai-065.explication: By directly capturing the left bundle branch, pacing rapidly activates the LV, while the RV is activated later: this produces a right-sided delay pattern in V1 (qR, rSR'). The time from stimulus to R-wave peak in V6 (LV activation time) is short and remains stable as output is varied. Commonly proposed thresholds are around 75 to 80 ms depending on the baseline QRS. An LBBB pattern with slow LV activation, on the contrary, reflects deep septal pacing without bundle branch capture. The transition between non-selective and selective capture is also a strong criterion.
prog-dai-065.aRetenir: LBBAP: right-sided delay in V1 and a short, stable LV activation time in V6.
